title: AFLW Salary: How to Convert Hourly Rates to Annual Pay in Australia
description: Understand how an AFLW salary or any hourly rate converts to annual pay. Includes tax, super, and the National Minimum Wage for 2026-27.
salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, an hourly rate of $26.44 gives an annual gross of $52,254.80, with super on top.

faqs.q: How is annual pay calculated from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply the hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week (typically 38 for full-time) and then by 52 weeks. For example, $30 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $59,280 per year. This assumes the same rate every week with no unpaid overtime or penalty rates.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage is the base rate for employees not covered by an award or agreement. From 1 July 2026 it is $26.44 per hour. Award rates are higher minimums set by industry or occupation. Most employees are covered by a modern award, so their minimum pay is the award rate, not the National Minimum Wage.

faqs.q: How is casual loading applied and does super apply on top?
faqs.a: Casual employees receive a 25% loading on their base rate. For the National Minimum Wage, that is $33.05 per hour. Superannuation is paid on top of the total ordinary earnings, including the casual loading, at 12% up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the AFLW Salary and Hourly Conversion

When you hear about an **aflw salary**, it is often quoted as an annual figure. But many roles, including part-time and casual positions, are paid by the hour. Converting an hourly rate to an annual salary helps you compare offers and understand your total compensation. This guide explains the standard formula, the role of the National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, superannuation, and tax.

### The Formula for Annual Pay

The basic calculation is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

We assume a full-time week is 38 ordinary hours, as defined by the Fair Work Commission. For example, if your hourly rate is $30, your annual gross pay would be $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This is before tax and super. The same formula applies whether you are looking at an **aflw salary** or any other hourly wage.

If you are paid fortnightly, your gross fortnight is the weekly amount multiplied by two. For the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour, the weekly pay is $1,004.90, so the fortnight is $2,009.80.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The Fair Work Commission sets the **National Minimum Wage** each year. From 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week. This is the minimum for employees not covered by an award or enterprise agreement.

Most workers, however, are covered by a modern award. Awards set higher minimum rates for specific industries and occupations. For example, the Social, Community, Home Care and Disability Services Award and the Supported Employment Services Award have their own pay guides. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes these pay guides, which include minimum rates, allowances, and penalty rates. Always check the correct award for your role rather than relying solely on the National Minimum Wage.

### Casual Loading and Superannuation

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of their base rate. For the National Minimum Wage, that is $33.05 per hour. This loading compensates for the lack of paid leave. When using our [the timesheet](/) tool, you can check a box to add the 25% casual loading. Never type a rate that already includes casual loading; the tool adds it for you.

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at the rate of 12% (from 1 July 2026). This applies to both the base rate and the casual loading. The super guarantee has a maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For example, on a $59,280 annual salary, the super contribution would be $7,113.60, paid by your employer in addition to your gross pay.

### Tax and Medicare Levy

Your annual gross pay is used to calculate income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Most taxpayers also pay a Medicare levy of 2% of taxable income. Low-income earners may have a reduced rate or be exempt. The tax-free threshold is included in the above brackets.

For an **aflw salary** of, say, $60,000 per year, the tax would be approximately $5,092 plus $1,200 Medicare levy (before any offsets). Your take-home pay would be around $53,708 per year, or $1,032 per week. Use our [pay guides](/blog) to see award-specific rates, or the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page for the base rate.

### Using the Timesheet Tool

Our [the timesheet](/) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and choose whether you are casual. It calculates your weekly, fortnightly, and annual gross pay, then estimates tax, Medicare, and super. The tool follows the same formula: hourly × hours per week × 52, with a default of 38 hours. You can adjust the hours if you work part-time.

Remember, this is an estimate. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax uses the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. Always consult a qualified professional for your personal situation.

### Summary

Whether you are evaluating an **aflw salary** or any other hourly offer, the conversion to annual pay is straightforward. Know your hourly rate, confirm your hours per week, and multiply by 52. Then factor in casual loading, super, and tax to understand your true take-home pay. Use the official sources – Fair Work Commission, Fair Work Ombudsman, Australian Bureau of Statistics, and Australian Taxation Office – for the most reliable figures.
